Learning Objectives
Review the diagnosis of cerebral palsy and its risk factors.
Effectively communicate functional ability in children with cerebral palsy.
Perform an appropriate physical assessment of children with cerebral palsy.
Recognize common gait deviations in ambulatory children with cerebral palsy.

musculoskeletal impairments, particularly in patients with less functional ability (level IV and
level V).
Be familiar with the orthopaedic management of deformity in children with cerebral palsy,
specifically the importance of selective muscle-tendon surgical management, management of
lever arm dysfunction, and the manner in which hip and spinal management differs in children

Overview
Cerebral palsy is the most common cause of motor disability in childhood.
The Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) allows for ready communication of
functional ability and predicts the likelihood of some musculoskeletal impairments.1
Epidemiology and Risk Factors
The incidence of cerebral palsy (CP) ranges from 1 to 3 per 1,000 live births and is slowly
rising.2
Prematurity, low birth weight (<1,500 g), and multiple gestations are the main risk factors for
the development of cerebral palsy.

Prematurity and low birth weight may reflect other deleterious factors in early fetal
development. Although some mothers may have a genetic predisposition to prematurity,
the exact relationship between specific genetic mutations and prematurity is
incompletely understood. The rates of cerebral palsy were increasing with improved care
of severely premature infants in the developed world; however, these rates currently
have stabilized.2

Despite these risk factors, most children with cerebral palsy are born full-term. At one
time, birth asphyxia was thought to be the main risk factor for cerebral palsy; however,
only a minority of infants with cerebral palsy have this history. The true risk factors for
cerebral palsy are thought to be white matter changes in the brain and structural
damage to brain parenchyma or ventricles. These anatomic lesions increase the risk of
cerebral palsy drastically. Other risk factors include chorioamnionitis, hypothyroxinemia,
hypocapnia, and intrauterine growth retardation. Preventive treatment options that
decrease the risk of cerebral palsy include magnesium sulfate administered to mothers
during labor with premature infants, and immediate brain-body cooling in infants with
birth asphyxia.3
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Cerebral palsy is a static encephalopathy: a nonprogressive, permanent injury to the fetal or
developing brain, affecting motor development, sensation, cognition, communication, and
behavior.3
Although the encephalopathy associated with cerebral palsy is static, the musculoskeletal
pathophysiology is dynamic and ever changing with a child’s growing skeleton.
Cerebral palsy may affect motor development, upper and lower extremities, cognition,
feeding, and sensation.
Children with cerebral palsy often have a combination of axial hypotonia (decreased muscle
tone) and appendicular hypertonia (increased tone).
Typically, muscles that cross two joints are most affected in patients with cerebral palsy (hip
flexors, adductors, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, biceps).
The diagnosis of cerebral palsy was historically based exclusively on clinical examination;
however, currently, brain MRI can be used to confirm the diagnosis of cerebral palsy.
Although not present in all children, those born premature often demonstrate periventricular
leukomalacia or intraventricular hemorrhage associated with prematurity on MRI.
Predominant white matter injury is associated with high rates of aided or unaided
ambulation,4,5 relatively low rates of intellectual disability, and epilepsy.4-6
The key feature of the musculoskeletal pathology in cerebral palsy is failure of longitudinal and
circumferential growth of skeletal muscle. In children with cerebral palsy, skeletal muscle does

not relax during activity because of spasticity, and the children have greatly reduced levels of
activity because of weakness and poor balance.7
A newborn child with cerebral palsy does not have contractures or lower limb deformities, and
most do not show signs of spasticity. With time, spasticity will develop, and the muscle-tendon
growth will lag behind bone growth and contractures will develop.8

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The official definition of cerebral palsy from an international workgroup is: “Cerebral
palsy describes a group of permanent disorders of the development of movement and
posture, causing activity limitation, that are attributed to non-progressive disturbances
that occurred in the developing fetal or infant brain. The motor disorders of cerebral
palsy are often accompanied by disturbances of sensation, perception, cognition,
communication and behavior, by epilepsy and by secondary musculoskeletal problems.9
Natural History
Motor development in children with cerebral palsy is known to improve until approximately
age 6 to 8 years, at which point gross motor function plateaus.10
Decline in functional ability can occur in the peri-adolescent or young adult years in children
functioning at GMFCS level III, level IV, or level V.
As children with cerebral palsy age, fixed contractures and skeletal deformity may develop.
Young ambulatory children typically present with an equinus or jump gait pattern in early
childhood; however, as they get older and heavier, this pattern may evolve into more of a
crouch-type gait pattern with or without a surgical procedure that weakens the Achilles
tendon.11
Adolescence is a key period of growth and transition for those with cerebral palsy. A mobility
decline may occur during adolescence, which may be attributed to the cumulative muscle
contractures and torsional abnormalities in combination with increasing size of the patient
and decreasing availability of services and therapies.12
Joint contractures in the lower limbs of patients functioning at GMFCS level II may increase
without treatment13

The natural history of gait may be progressive deterioration, including increasing stiffness
throughout the lower limb joints and increasing tendency to flexed knee gait and ultimately
crouched gait.12,14 The transition from equinus gait to crouched gait often is accelerated by
procedures that weaken the gastrocnemius-soleus complex, especially lengthening of the
Achilles tendons.11
A therapeutic window for spasticity management before the development of fixed
contractures has been thought to exist;15 however, whether spasticity management results in
improvements in mobility or quality of life compared with minimal spasticity management
remains unknown.16 In addition, whether reduction of spasticity results in less orthopaedic
surgery, specifically contracture surgery, remains unclear.17
A second therapeutic window exists for the correction of fixed contracture and
musculoskeletal deformities before the onset of decompensation.18

Natural History
Adolescence is a key period of transition in the function of many children with cerebral
palsy. Many children with greater functional limitations will lose independent mobility
during this period, most substantially those functioning at GMFCS level IV. Theories for
this decline include puberty and growth, increase in patient size, patient effort,
increasing environmental demands in the community, and decreased available therapies
and services.12
Classification
Several classification systems are useful in communicating impairments in cerebral palsy.
Anatomic
The location of the brain injury in cerebral palsy causes different types of motor dysfunction.
Injury to the pyramidal tracts or periventricular regions of the brain often lead to spasticity,
defined as a velocity-dependent resistance to passive musculotendinous stretch.

Extrapyramidal brain injury (eg, basal ganglia) is less common and may lead to dyskinesia, a
term that includes involuntary movements, athetosis, and dystonia.
Patients can have mixed-type cerebral palsy, implying combined spastic and dyskinetic motor
patterns.
Geographic Pattern
The peripheral manifestations in cerebral palsy can be classified as bilateral or unilateral,
depending on the brain injury pattern. Terms to communicate motor involvement include the
following:
Diplegia: bilateral lower extremity involvement
Hemiplegia: one side of the body involvement, upper and lower extremity
Quadriplegia: all four extremities involved, often lower extremities more than the upper
extremities
Functional
For ambulant children with cerebral palsy, the most important functional classification
schemes are the GMFCS (Figure 1) and the Functional Mobility Scale.10,19
These two classification schemes attempt to quantify mobility for children with cerebral palsy
in their everyday environment.

Patients with spastic-type (pyramidal) cerebral palsy exhibit increased tone or rigidity with
rapid stretching, which may lead to disturbances in gait. These patients most often benefit
from orthopaedic treatment.
Patients with dyskinetic (extrapyramidal) or choreoathetoid cerebral palsy exhibit involuntary
movements, athetosis, and dystonia. This type of cerebral palsy is less frequently observed
than pyramidal cerebral palsy with the administration of Rh immune globulin to pregnant
women to prevent Rh incompatibility between mothers and their infants.
Patients with ataxia (cerebellar) exhibit disturbed balance and coordination.
Patients with mixed types of cerebral palsy show spasticity and dyskinesia.
Orthopaedic surgeons generally observe and manage the sequelae of spasticity; however, they
should be aware that other motor pathologies may coexist with spasticity, contractures, and
bony torsions.
These other pathologies may affect the ultimate outcome of surgical and nonsurgical
management.

Physiologic
The terms diplegia, hemiplegia, and quadriplegia are being supplanted by unilateral and
bilateral cerebral palsy because often bilateral but asymmetric motor involvement is
present, for which the term hemiplegia is misleading. A better term for this clinical
pattern may be asymmetric bilateral cerebral palsy.
The GMFCS is an important method of communication between healthcare providers;
however, it also predicts the likelihood of certain musculoskeletal impairments, such as
hip subluxation. Using the GMFCS, other ordinal classification systems have been
developed for easily communicating upper extremity function, communication ability,
and feeding ability.21
Before the GMFCS was developed, many outcome studies were published using the
Gillette Functional Assessment Questionnaire22 and the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of
North America Outcomes Data Collection Instrument.23 These instruments have been

In typical development, femoral anteversion is thought to be 45° at birth and to decrease
throughout growth until final anteversion of 10° to 15°, with most remodeling occurring
by age 8 years and some modest remodeling reported thereafter. Tibial torsion begins
with internal rotation and remodels into external rotation in almost all situations and all
diagnoses, with or without management.
Note that little correlation may exist between the static physical examination and
corresponding gait deviations. For example, the popliteal angle measurement (a
surrogate of hamstring contracture) has almost no relationship with the degree of
crouched gait. The magnitude of femoral anteversion observed during physical
examination (trochanteric prominence angle test) is poorly correlated with true
anteversion. The preferred method for quantification is diagnostic imaging studies (CT,
MRI, biplanar radiography). The numeric value of the femoral anteversion of a limb on
physical examination and imaging studies also is poorly correlated with hip rotation on
gait kinematics.

myelomeningocele. Instrumented motion analysis, measuring kinematic dynamic joint range
of motion, kinetic parameters (moments and power), electromyography (EMG) muscle activity,
foot plantar pressure, and energy expenditure allows for improved treatment plans and
evaluation of the efficacy of surgical management and orthotics.

Gait Analysis
Instrumented gait analysis can be used to identify primary, secondary, and
compensatory motions that are not apparent via video analysis alone. Cited studies are
useful resources for in-depth review of the gait cycle27 and pathologic gait patterns and
their management in patients with cerebral palsy.28
Davids et al29 described a diagnostic matrix, in which all clinical, radiographic, and gait
data are incorporated into decision making for an individual ambulatory patient with
cerebral palsy (Figure 13). This includes intraoperative updating of a surgical plan based
on the examination under anesthesia because deformities, particularly muscular
deformities, may change after bony corrections are performed. For example, a distal
femoral extension osteotomy may change the relative length of the gastrocnemius,
which inserts on the posterior aspect of the distal femur. (Resource 2)

BoNT-A Basic Concepts
Injection of skeletal muscle with BoNT-A results in a dose-dependent, partially reversible
chemodenervation by blocking presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular
junction.3
Strong evidence suggests that the injection of BoNT-A results in a reduction in muscle stiffness
as measured by the Modified Ashworth Scale and a reduction is spasticity as measured by the
Modified Tardieu Scale. This has been confirmed in multiple randomized clinical trials and
cohort studies.36-40
The paradox of clinical trials on BoNT-A is that strong evidence suggests improvement in
surrogate outcomes (Modified Ashworth Scale and Modified Tardieu Scale) and weak or no
evidence suggests improvement in clinically relevant outcomes.41-43
In the past decade, a large body of research has been performed in small mammals, including
mice, rats, and rabbits, investigating the effects of BoNT-A injections.3
These studies have reported similar findings, which can be summarized as follows: Injection of
BoNT-A in animal models is followed by acute muscle atrophy, replacement of contractile
elements of muscle with fat, and upregulation of molecular pathways leading to fibrosis.44,45
Indications for BoNT-A
BoNT-A should only be used to manage dynamic spasticity. In patients with fixed contractures,
surgical treatment should be considered.
For ambulatory children (<5 years) who present with spastic equinus, typical first-line
management involves injections of BoNT-A as children begin to stand and commence walking,
often between age 1 and 3 years.36-38 Injections usually are combined with physical therapy
and the use of an AFO.3,46 Serial cast immobilization in combination with this treatment also
may be considered.
Note that BoNT-A has not been approved by the FDA for use in patients younger than 18
years. Such use is off-label, and BoNT-A should not be used in children younger than 2 years.
In adults, BoNT-A is FDA approved only for upper-extremity spasticity.

Contraindications for BoNT-A
The primary effect of injection of BoNT-A is skeletal muscle atrophy. The reduction in spasticity
is secondary to muscle atrophy. Muscle atrophy and weakness is a most undesirable
consequence in a condition such as cerebral palsy, which is characterized by weakness.47

frequency should be restricted to a maximum of once per 12 months.

Pelvic obliquity and scoliosis also are common findings in nonambulatory patients that need to
be assessed during physical examination. Unmanaged pelvic obliquity may result in re-
displacement of the hips postoperatively. Windblown deformities of the hip also may result
from abduction contracture of one hip and adduction contracture of the other hip, leading to
considerable pelvic obliquity.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
An AP radiograph of the pelvis is most commonly used to assess hip dysplasia in children with
cerebral palsy.
Migration percentage is the main parameter measured on hip radiographs in children with
cerebral palsy and quantifies lateral displacement of the hip (Figure 17).

necessary to flatten the lumbar lordosis. Another method to compensate for a hip flexion

developed to screen children at risk.

The frequency of screening depends on the age and functional level of the child.
Initially, hip displacement may be asymptomatic in children with cerebral palsy and symptoms
may only be observed if the hips are dislocated and arthritic. Hip surveillance programs have
been developed to monitor the progression of hip displacement in the at-risk population so
appropriate management can be performed to attain painless, mobile, and located hips in
children and adults with cerebral palsy.
Scandinavian, Australian, and British Columbia models of hip surveillance have been reported
in the literature. These programs require a series of physical examinations and screening AP
pelvis radiographs, with their frequency depending on age, migration percentage, and GMFCS
level.
Patients with GMFCS level I require the least frequent hip surveillance unless they are
classified as hemiplegic with hip involvement (type IV hemiplegia; Figure 16).
In most surveillance programs, orthopaedic referral is recommended if the migration
percentage is greater than 30%. Screening radiographs typically begin at age 24 months and
end at skeletal maturity. Patients with scoliosis, pelvic obliquity, and a migration percentage
greater than 30% require screening radiographs even after skeletal maturity.72,73
Other Imaging Studies
Occasionally, CT is performed to assess the location and degree of acetabular deficiency or to
determine version if the patient is ambulatory.
CT also is useful in identifying rare anterior hip dislocations that may otherwise be missed on
radiographs.
CT may be helpful in the preoperative assessment, especially if uncertainty exists with regard
to the location and degree of acetabular deficiency. By providing a better assessment of the
acetabular deficiency, CT may help determine the type of acetabular procedures necessary
during hip reconstruction surgery. CT also may aid in the assessment of proximal femur
geometry and femoral anteversion.74
Management
Because hip dysplasia is progressive during childhood and adolescence in patients with
cerebral palsy, management is recommended if screening radiographs show a migration
percentage greater than 30%. Management can be broadly categorized as nonsurgical or
surgical treatment options.

Surgical treatment options are further divided into soft-tissue, reconstruction, and salvage
procedures.
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management does not prevent the progression of hip dysplasia.
Nonsurgical management in the form of abduction bracing and BoNT-A injection to the hip
adductors has been reported in the literature. Although these methods increase hip range of
motion, they do not prevent progression of hip dysplasia in children with cerebral palsy.
Their main role is in improving hip abduction to allow for better perineal care.72,73
Surgical Management
Surgical management of hip displacement in patients with cerebral palsy is divided into soft-
tissue, hip reconstruction, and salvage procedures.
Soft-tissue Procedures
Soft-tissue procedures involve releasing the contracted hip adductors and, in some patients,
the iliopsoas.
Isolated soft-tissue procedures are indicated in young children (younger than 6 years) with a
migration percentage between 30% and 60% and contracture of the hip adductors.

Soft-tissue Procedures
Soft-tissue procedures aim to decrease the asymmetric forces on the hip joint by
releasing the spastic and contracted hip adductors. Improving perineal care is another
goal of these procedures. Soft-tissue procedures involve complete release of the
adductor longus and gracilis. Release of anterior fibers of the adductor brevis also may
be performed in nonambulatory children if release of the adductor longus and gracilis
does not lead to adequate hip abduction (>45°). In patients with cerebral palsy, the
anterior branch of the obturator nerve, which courses on the anterior surface of the
adductor brevis, is identified and protected. Destruction of this nerve may result in an
abduction contracture, which often is difficult to manage. Adductor release in isolation is
only indicated in young children (younger than 6 years) with a migration percentage

Reconstruction procedures are indicated if the migration percentage is greater than 40% in

Reconstruction procedures include proximal femur varus osteotomy. Acetabular osteotomy
also should be performed if residual acetabular dysplasia is present.

Reconstruction Procedures
Hip reconstruction in children with cerebral palsy includes a proximal femur osteotomy.
Reconstruction procedures are indicated if the migration percentage is greater than 40%
in children older than 6 years and if the migration percentage is greater than 60% in
children younger than 6 years. Soft-tissue releases also typically are performed at the
time of hip reconstruction. The goal of proximal femur osteotomy is to correct proximal
femur bony abnormalities, which include coxa valga and increased femoral anteversion.
The goal is to achieve a femoral neck-shaft angle of 90° to 100° in nonambulatory
children (GMFCS level IV or level V) and a femoral neck-shaft angle of 120° in ambulatory
patients (GMFCS level I to level III). Some femoral shortening typically is performed
depending on the degree of hip displacement.
Acetabular osteotomies also can be performed if acetabular dysplasia is present
(acetabular index >25). San Diego–style acetabular osteotomies are preferred in children
with spastic hip dislocation to manage the posterolateral acetabular deficiency that
typically is present.72,73 An arthrogram can be obtained at the time of surgery to confirm
reduction and to assess the need for open hip reduction and capsulorrhaphy.

If painful degenerative arthritis of the hip is present, reconstruction procedures are no longer
indicated and salvage procedures should be considered. Salvage procedures include proximal
femur resection, proximal femur valgus osteotomy, and total hip arthroplasty.
Proximal femur resection involves resection of the proximal femur right below the lesser
trochanter. This procedure may be considered in nonambulatory patients with degenerative
arthritis and painful dislocated hips. As long as 1 year may be required after this procedure
before the patient experiences pain relief.72,73 Complications include heterotopic ossification
and proximal migration of the femur.
Proximal femur valgus osteotomy is indicated if limited hip abduction rather than pain is the
main functional problem. This procedure improves hip abduction by placing the femoral head
farther from the acetabulum. The procedure also can be performed in combination with
femoral head resection if pain also is present (McHale procedure).72,73 Similar to proximal
femur resection, this procedure is not indicated in ambulatory patients. Complications include
symptomatic hardware and nonunion.
Total hip replacement should be considered in ambulatory patients with painful arthritic
dysplastic hips.72,73
Outcomes
The success of isolated soft-tissue procedures depends on the amount of hip displacement
and the level of function.
Guided growth procedures for the proximal femur to correct hip valgus are gaining popularity;
however, the long-term success of this method is not yet clear.
Hip reconstruction procedures may lead to improvement in pain associated with dislocation
observed in some patients.
The results of salvage procedures are inferior to those of hip reconstruction procedures.
Soft-tissue procedures are associated with an 83% success rate if the migration percentage is
less than or equal to 40% and a 23% success rate if the migration percentage is greater than
40%.75 A study of children with cerebral palsy managed via isolated adductor release reported
a 32% success rate after 8 years.76
A study found the success rate was related to the level of function and ambulation, with a 94%
success rate in GMCSF level I or level II patients compared with a 14% success rate in GMFCS
level V patients. Another study reported a higher success rate (67%) with soft-tissue
procedures.72,73,77
